top_slots.interpretation: Slot 0 on RaptureElement is FUN_004DEB40 (destructor). The 4 callers using slot 0 are all teardown paths: FUN_0054c160 config unbind, FUN_00765340 list erase, FUN_0075bec0 single destroy via Lua binding, FUN_004dc690 case 0xCB RemoveActor.

Slot 9 on RaptureElement is FUN_0091F6F0 (set parent context per the actor-map-writers pass). The sole user is FUN_004dc690's generic Actor-cluster fallthrough (BCS-Y-0527). The actor-vftable9-investigation and actor-vtable9-bulk passes confirmed this is NOT an opcode handler; on RaptureElement instances it sets *(this+0x18) and calls FUN_00571bb0(this, 0).
Slot 11 on RaptureElement is FUN_0091C5B0 (trampoline to slot[0x30]). Called by FUN_0054c160 before the slot-0 destructor - probably a pre-destroy notify hook.

Slot 8 on RaptureElement is FUN_0091C520 (small helper per the actor-map-writers pass dump). Called by FUN_004daa10 with (opcode_index, msg_buf, value) - the queued-message receiver. Most interesting non-trivial slot use: this is a candidate for examination as the per-actor 'apply queued state change' entrypoint.

struct_offset_histogram.note: Counts how many callers read/write specific offsets on the FUN_004d9910 return value. Most callers don't touch struct fields directly - they dispatch via vtable or discard the result.

The actor's struct fields are accessed predominantly *inside* slot-0/8/9 implementations or in supporting helpers, not at the caller-of-004d9910 layer.

classification_histogram.interpretation: 28 of 43 callers are thin Lua wrappers in the 0x0075bXXX cluster that call FUN_004d9910(*param_1) for argument validation/side-effect and then dispatch a separate Lua handler. The actor pointer returned is discarded - the wrappers care only that the lookup succeeded (an exists check is implicit; failure becomes 0 which the helpers handle).
Four callers use the actor pointer to invoke its vtable[0] destructor. All four are teardown paths.

Three callers write to fields adjacent to a FUN_004d9910-derived variable, but only one (FUN_004dc690) is unambiguously writing to the actor pointer itself (+0x92 alive flag in case 0xCA AddActor). The other two (FUN_007694d0, FUN_00774ad0) actually write to *helper structs* derived from the actor in subsequent steps - the variable-tracking heuristic conflated them.

Three callers exhibit the 'find-or-create' pattern: lookup with FUN_004d9910, if NULL then create via FUN_004d90c0 (BCS-Y-0531). They are FUN_00774ad0 (Lua actor bind), FUN_004dc690 case 0xCA (s2c AddActor), FUN_0075be50 (system actor 0xc0000024 lazy init).
Two callers pass the actor pointer to another function without dispatching its vtable: FUN_004d9d70 (popup) -> FUN_004ddcf0/FUN_00927fa0, FUN_0055d990 (paired ref) -> FUN_004d72a0.
FUN_0075bbd0 returns the lookup result as bool. Used by 4 Lua-side callers as 'does this actor id exist?' check.

proposed_bcs_y_entries.name: ZoneActor_QueuedMessageDispatcher_FUN_004daa10
proposed_bcs_y_entries.summary: Per-frame zone actor message-queue dispatcher. Walks the queue at zone+0x17938..+0x17944 via FUN_004ddb50 (queue iterator) + InterlockedExchangeAdd / InterlockedExchange / InterlockedDecrement (lock-free pop). For each entry with type field != 2: extracts (uVar5 = *(entry+0x14) - 3) as a relative opcode/method index in [0, 0x101), reads actor_id from entry+0x10, looks up actor via FUN_004d9910 (BCS-Y-0534), and dispatches `actor->vtable[0x20](uVar5, entry+0x20, *(entry+0x18))` (slot 8). For type==2 entries: dispatches the slot-0x18 method on zone+0x17924 (the queue's output writer vtable). Concludes with a teardown step via `(*zone+0x17920)->vtable[0x14]() then FUN_00929b70 / FUN_005527a0 / FUN_004da680`.

Identifies vtable slot 8 (offset 0x20) of RaptureElement as the queued-message receiver method - the only non-destructor, non-lifecycle slot in active use across the catalog. Connects zone+0x17924/+0x17920 (queue output/input writer vtables) to actor dispatch. Sole caller is FUN_004b3c50 (likely the per-tick dispatcher caller).

Garbage-collection-style sweep that prunes Lua refs to vanished actors.
proposed_bcs_y_entries.rationale: Demonstrates a third distinct use of FUN_004d9910 as a liveness check (after thin-wrapper validation and existence-predicate). Provides RTTI evidence linking the Lua control list to CharaBase actors specifically.

proposed_bcs_y_entries.name: LuaActorExistencePredicate_FUN_0075bbd0
proposed_bcs_y_entries.summary: Smallest caller (23 bytes). Pure predicate: `return FUN_004d9910(*param_1) != 0`. Used by 4 Lua-side callers (FUN_006cc760, FUN_006d8f30, FUN_006d9570, FUN_006e3a60) as the canonical 'does this actor id resolve to a live actor?' check.
proposed_bcs_y_entries.rationale: Architectural primitive - the simplest form of FUN_004d9910 consumption. Worth a catalog entry as the canonical pattern.

proposed_bcs_y_entries.name: LuaActorBindingThinWrapperCluster_0x0075b7XX_0x0075beXX
proposed_bcs_y_entries.summary: 30 thin Lua-binding wrappers in the 0x0075b7XX..0x0075beXX address range, each ~24-44 bytes. Common shape: `FUN_004d9910(*param_1); FUN_005XXXXX(param_2..N);` - validate actor exists via lookup (result discarded), then dispatch a specific Lua-callable helper in the 0x0053XXXX cluster (FUN_005354d0, FUN_005355a0, FUN_00535670, etc.). These are auto-generated C-wrappers exposing zone-actor methods to Lua scripts.
proposed_bcs_y_entries.rationale: Bulk-catalog the 30 thin wrappers as a single cluster entry rather than 30 individual BCS-Y entries. Their volume (~70% of FUN_004d9910 callers) and structural homogeneity argue for cluster treatment. Future per-wrapper detail can be cataloged as needed when each helper FUN_005XXXXX is characterized.

key_findings.title: 65% of FUN_004d9910 callers are thin Lua-binding wrappers that discard the result
key_findings.detail: 28 of 43 callers (and 30 if you include the 2 more substantive ones with the same shape) are 24-44 byte functions in the 0x0075b7XX..0x0075beXX cluster. Each invokes FUN_004d9910(*param_1) as input validation, discards the result, and proceeds to call a specific FUN_005XXXXX (typically 0x0053XXXX range) helper. This is an auto-generated Lua C-binding pattern that exposes zone-actor methods to scripts.
key_findings.implication: The actor map lookup primitive's primary visible role is argument validation for the Lua API surface - not direct actor mutation. The 44-caller count overstates the architectural surface; real actor-pointer-consuming code paths are ~13.

key_findings.title: Only 4 callers dispatch actor vtable slot 0 (destructor); only the dispatcher (FUN_004dc690) dispatches slot 9 or slot 8
key_findings.detail: Vtable dispatches via the FUN_004d9910 return value: slot 0 (destructor) = 4 callers (FUN_0054c160 config-unbind, FUN_00765340 list-erase, FUN_0075bec0 Lua-binding destroy, FUN_004dc690 case 0xCB RemoveActor); slot 9 (offset 0x24) = 1 caller (FUN_004dc690 generic fallthrough = BCS-Y-0527); slot 8 (offset 0x20) = 1 caller (FUN_004daa10 queued-message dispatcher); slot 11 (offset 0x2c) = 1 caller (FUN_0054c160 pre-destroy hook). No caller dispatches slot 5 (lifecycle hook).
key_findings.implication: The actor's vtable is dispatched from only a small number of well-defined call sites. The 'queued-message dispatcher' role of slot 8 (FUN_004daa10) is the most architecturally novel finding - a previously-unknown per-frame actor-message-queue system parallel to the s2c packet dispatcher.

key_findings.title: FUN_004daa10 reveals a per-frame queued-message dispatch system separate from s2c packet dispatch
key_findings.detail: FUN_004daa10 walks a queue at zone+0x17938..+0x17944 (lock-free via Interlocked ops), and for each entry dispatches `actor->vtable[0x20](opcode_index, msg_buf, value)` (slot 8) on the actor recovered via FUN_004d9910. This is structurally a SECOND dispatcher (in addition to FUN_004dc690) that targets specific actors with per-actor opcode-indexed methods. Sole caller FUN_004b3c50 (the per-tick caller).
key_findings.implication: Resolves an open question from the actor-vftable9-investigation / actor-factory-drill / actor-vtable9-bulk passes: the architecture has a SECOND actor-dispatch path that doesn't go through FUN_004dc690. The Actor cluster opcodes (0x0F + 0xCC..0xE5) handled by FUN_004dc690's generic fallthrough via slot 9 (no-op stub) MAY actually be processed indirectly via this queued-message system AFTER being queued by some intermediate handler. Worth a future phase: drill FUN_004b3c50 (caller of FUN_004daa10) to confirm the queue's source - whether it's fed by FUN_004dc690 (via case-7 or another case) or by an external producer (network thread enqueuing directly).

key_findings.title: No NEW opcode-processing handler exists among the 43 callers
key_findings.detail: Only FUN_004dc690 (already cataloged as BCS-Y-0279) exhibits a switch(opcode) structure with FUN_004d9910 lookups inside the cases. The 42 other callers do not switch on packet bytes. The thin wrappers, system-actor helpers, list iterators, and predicates all use FUN_004d9910 for either argument validation or specific actor management - not packet processing.
key_findings.implication: Refutes any hypothesis that a hidden opcode handler exists in the FUN_004d9910 caller set. The Actor cluster opcodes' processing pathway is confined to FUN_004dc690's generic fallthrough (vtable[9] no-op + queue-up?) or the still-uncharacterized FUN_004daa10 queue source.

key_findings.title: Three system-actor ids empirically mapped by purpose
key_findings.detail: (1) 0xc0000004 = Camera system actor (FUN_0054b680 registers RaptureCommands.MoveCamera/ForwardCameraOff/BackwardCameraOff callbacks); (2) 0xc0000020 = Popup/menu system actor (FUN_004d9d70 dispatches to it for one popup type); (3) 0xc0000024 = unknown but instantiated from class 0x1a (FUN_0075be50 lazy-init). All three are in the 'engine-managed' id range (top byte 0xC0..0xDF per BCS-Y-0533 FUN_004d9030's pattern).
key_findings.implication: Provides the first empirical id->purpose mappings for engine-managed system actors. Future phase can drill class 0x1a and the camera-actor's vtable to identify the C++ types behind these ids.

key_findings.title: The 'lazy_init_create_if_absent' (find-or-create) pattern appears 3 times
key_findings.detail: (1) FUN_004dc690 case 0xCA AddActor (find-or-create from network packet); (2) FUN_00774ad0 Lua actor bind (find-or-create with class 0x1a default); (3) FUN_0075be50 lazy init for 0xc0000024. All three use the same FUN_004d9910 -> FUN_004d90c0 fallback structure.
key_findings.implication: Confirms FUN_004d90c0 (BCS-Y-0531) as the canonical 'create' counterpart to FUN_004d9910's 'find'. The pattern is consistent across both network-driven (case 0xCA) and Lua-driven (FUN_00774ad0) and bootstrap (FUN_0075be50) contexts.

key_findings.title: Actor field offset writes via the FUN_004d9910 return are limited to +0x92 (alive flag) in case 0xCA AddActor
key_findings.detail: The only unambiguous direct write to an actor field through the FUN_004d9910-derived pointer is FUN_004dc690's case 0xCA setting *(actor + 0x92) = 1 (the alive byte). Other 'modifies_actor_fields' classifications (FUN_007694d0, FUN_00774ad0) are heuristic false positives where the offsets are on related helper structs (iVar8 from FUN_0076a3f0 etc.), not on the actor itself.
key_findings.implication: Reinforces the BCS-Y-0525 case 0xCA description: AddActor sets the alive flag at +0x92 on the actor pointer recovered from the map (whether the actor was just created or was found pre-existing). No other actor fields are mutated at this dispatcher layer.

open_questions.q: What feeds the queue at zone+0x17938..+0x17944 that FUN_004daa10 dispatches?
open_questions.approach: Drill the caller FUN_004b3c50 plus all writers of zone+0x17938/+0x1793c/+0x17944 (likely InterlockedExchange/InterlockedExchangeAdd producers). If the network thread or s2c dispatcher (FUN_004dc690) enqueues into this queue, it would explain how Actor cluster opcodes get processed despite the slot-9 stub. Candidate work for a future pass.

open_questions.q: What is class 0x1a (the class id FUN_0075be50 and FUN_00774ad0 lazy-create with)?
open_questions.approach: Drill FUN_004d90c0 (BCS-Y-0531) with input class_id=0x1a to identify the actor class instantiated. Class 0x1a is in the 'regular' id range (not 0xC0..0xDF) so it bypasses the FUN_00d35af0 registry check; it must be a class index into the method table at zone+0x10.

open_questions.q: What does vtable slot 8 (FUN_0091C520) on RaptureElement actually do?
open_questions.approach: The actor-map-writers pass noted slot 8 = FUN_0091C520 'small helper'. This reveals it's the queued-message receiver. Decomp FUN_0091C520 directly to characterize the message handler protocol (what does the (opcode_index, msg_buf, value) tuple parse into?). Quick candidate for a follow-up pass.

open_questions.q: Why does FUN_00765340 call FUN_004d9910 twice per iteration?
open_questions.approach: Pattern: 1st lookup, condition check via FUN_00535ce0, 2nd lookup, destroy. The double-lookup is unusual - either defensive against intervening invalidation (some FUN_00535ce0 side effect?) or a decompiler artifact. Quick disassembly inspection at 0x00765340 would clarify.

phase_assessment: Complete. Bulk-decomp + classification of all 43 FUN_004d9910 callers produced a clear architectural map. Main finding is the discovery of FUN_004daa10 as a SECOND actor-message dispatcher (queue-based, parallel to the network packet dispatcher FUN_004dc690), with vtable slot 8 as its target on RaptureElement actors. This opens a path for a future pass to resolve the open question from the actor-vftable9-investigation / actor-factory-drill / actor-vtable9-bulk passes about Actor cluster opcode processing. Also empirically mapped 3 engine-managed system actor ids by purpose and confirmed the 65/35 split between thin Lua wrappers and substantive callers. 10 proposed BCS-Y entries identified but NOT applied (manifest is draft-only per task constraints; symbols.json untouched).
